title.en: What the Charter's first words say
title.fr: Ce que disent les premiers mots de la Charte

text.en: Canada's Charter of Rights and Freedoms opens with a line that puts the supremacy of God beside the rule of law. Those first words matter in two ways: they say religious traditions have a place in Canadian society, and they say each human being has dignity and worth.
text.fr: La Charte canadienne des droits et libertés s'ouvre sur une phrase qui place la suprématie de Dieu à côté de la primauté du droit. Ces premiers mots comptent de deux façons : ils disent que les traditions religieuses ont leur place dans la société canadienne, et que chaque être humain a une dignité et une valeur.

source.quote: the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which begins with the words, “Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law.” This phrase underlines the importance of religious traditions to Canadian society and the dignity and worth of the human person.

verification.evidence: The Constitution of Canada was amended in 1982 to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which begins with the words, “Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law.” This phrase underlines the importance of religious traditions to Canadian society and the dignity and worth of the human person.
